summary: Revises the sample timeline for the Nominating and Recall Committee process described in RFC 3777. Recent committees had found the old schedule hard to follow, so this adjusts the timeline. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7437.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a revised calendar for how the IETF picks its leaders. Earlier calendars did not fit well, so the dates were rearranged. It was replaced by RFC 7437.

questions: how does the ietf nomcom timeline work
iesg and iab selection process timeline
how does the ietf pick its leaders

subtitle: A revised calendar for how the IETF picks its leaders.

tldr.problem: RFC 3777 defined the IETF's Nominating and Recall Committee (NomCom) process and included a tight schedule that did not account for real-world delays like holidays, informal practices, and meetings. Recent NomCom chairs reported the timeline was unrealistic and unachievable.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a more realistic timeline that starts three months earlier than the original. It keeps all the normative requirements from RFC 3777 but spreads tasks across more calendar time, allowing each step the duration it actually takes.
tldr.outcome: NomComs can now organize and work at a sustainable pace. The timeline allows volunteers to meet face-to-face with the committee early and with nominees later, improving the quality of nominations. RFC 7437 later replaced this with further refinements.

today: RFC 5078 is Informational and updates RFC 3777's timeline only. It was later obsoleted by RFC 7437 in January 2015, which made further adjustments. However, the principle of allowing adequate time for each phase remains central to the NomCom process.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RFC 3777 defined the Nominating and Recall Committee (NomCom) process, which selects leaders for the IETF, the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). It included a sample timeline that met all the normative (mandatory) time requirements.

However, recent NomCom chairs reported the timeline was extremely aggressive. It did not account for real-world factors: people are on holiday between November and January, informal practices like notifying unsuccessful nominees take time, and the 30-day volunteer solicitation often stretches to 6 weeks in reality.

Additionally, volunteers are only announced after an IETF meeting, giving them little time to organize before the next meeting (the third IETF of the year), when they should be finishing their work. This forces heavy reliance on remote teleconferences.
sections.plainLanguage: The old calendar was like trying to move while it is raining and everyone is on holiday. The new calendar adds buffer time.

sections.title: The Revised Timeline
sections.content:
The solution is simple: start three months earlier. The ISOC president appoints the NomCom chair around May, not August. This lets the committee:

  • Announce and recruit volunteers with a full 6 weeks (not 30 days).
  • Have 6 weeks (not 4) for committee self-organization and planning.
  • Conduct candidate selection over 17 weeks (not 12), removing scheduling pressure.
  • Meet face-to-face with the committee during the second IETF instead of scrambling to organize remotely.
  • Spend time with nominees and refine choices before the third IETF.
  • Notify unsuccessful candidates privately one week before the public announcement.

Every time interval in RFC 3777 is still met. No normative requirements change. The new timeline just redistributes them across more calendar time.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of starting in August, start in May. The total time is the same, but work is spread out so nothing is rushed.

sections.title: Interaction with IETF Meetings
sections.content:
The IETF holds three meetings per year (roughly March, July, and November). The new timeline aligns NomCom milestones with these meetings, giving the committee face-to-face opportunities.

Under the old schedule: the second IETF meeting happened while volunteers were being solicited, and the third IETF came near the end of candidate selection.

Under the new schedule: the ISOC president identifies a NomCom chair candidate by the first IETF (March). The chair is appointed and begins work by late May. Volunteers are recruited and announced by the second IETF (July), when the committee can meet in person. Candidate selection happens July through January, with another face-to-face opportunity at the third IETF in November.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee can now sit down together three times a year to plan and meet nominees, instead of mostly talking on the phone.

sections.title: Sample 2008–2009 Timeline
sections.content:
The RFC includes a detailed table for the 2008–2009 NomCom. Key dates:

  • May 25, 2008: NomCom chair appointed, publishes milestones.
  • June 1 – July 13, 2008: Six-week solicitation for volunteers.
  • July 27, 2008: NomCom membership confirmed at the second IETF meeting.
  • August 3 – September 14, 2008: Committee self-organization and planning (six weeks).
  • September 21, 2008 – January 18, 2009: Candidate selection (17 weeks).
  • January 18 – February 15, 2009: Confirmation by IAB and IESG; notify unsuccessful nominees privately.
  • February 22, 2009: Public announcement of the slate, one month before the first IETF.

This allows time for unexpected delays and provides realistic buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: The old schedule had everything crammed into a few months. The new one spreads it across the full year.

sections.title: Observations and Nuances
sections.content:
The RFC notes some nuances. When NomCom starts earlier, the requirement for committee members to have attended 3 of the last 5 IETF meetings shifts earlier too, making different people eligible. Additionally, some IESG and IAB members take one-year terms; under the new schedule, they have only one IETF cycle to build a track record before NomCom evaluates them.

The RFC also mentions that future changes to RFC 3777 could allow the call for volunteers to be issued while the NomCom chair is still being selected, eliminating the serialized delay. The outgoing chair could issue the call on behalf of the incoming chair.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting earlier means some people are not yet eligible to volunteer, and new people become eligible. Edge cases like one-year terms need careful handling.

references.text: Galvin, J., "IAB and IESG Selection, Confirmation, and Recall Process: Operation of the Nominating and Recall Committees", BCP 10, RFC 3777, June 2004.
